utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday. I'd like to greet the accused, their Defence counsel, the OTP representatives, as well as everybody assisting us. I believe that Mr. Scott has a housekeeping matter to raise. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I'm once again hidden from Judge Trechsel behind the pole. Good morning to everyone else in the courtroom. Your Honours, I feel I must perhaps try the Chamber's patience just a bit this morning in the following respect: I spent a good deal of last evening going through my outline on this witness and reviewing again the various materials that the Prosecution prepared to use with this witness. I can tell the Chamber that as a result of my work last evening, I have reduced my outline considerably and, in fact, I will forgo a number of documents that I think are significant and of course I would prefer to put them before the Chamber but nonetheless given the time constraints, I have eliminated a significant number of them. Having said this, Your Honour, and given the number of topics that have been raised in the Defence examinations, I believe again as a result of my review that at bare minimum that I can responsibly deal with this witness, I'm asking the Chamber for an additional one hour of time to complete -- to complete my cross-examination. I thought it, Your Honours, important with this witness and I hope Your Honours agree that given a number of the issues that have been raised in particular with this witness, and his position at the relevant time that there were some issues that had to be dealt with at some length. And the Chamber will note that with the exception of yesterday afternoon which I do agree that I intervened more with the witness than in the afternoon but primarily during his examination I have not intervened extensively with the witness and I've let him give the full answers for the most part that he wanted to give. I cite as one example something that I thought should be put before the Chamber but took a fair amount of time was dealing with the rules of procedure of the Presidency yesterday which under the circumstances required that the witness read those out for translation. I think -- I hope the Chamber found that to be helpful and that information and to have that information -- evidence in front of it. That did take a considerable amount of the Prosecution's time. The Defence, Your Honours, with this witness had according to the registry 8 hours and 11 minutes and with the greatest respect, I don't see why the Prosecution's time should be considerably less than that. And I note because I went back and again reviewed this trial's statistics this morning, I note that during the Prosecution case there were a significant number of occasions where the Defence cross-examinations were not only equal to but in fact substantially longer than the Prosecution direct. For all those reasons, Your Honour, I am asking the Chamber for additional time. I think even with the additional time, and I think allowing for a reasonable time for any redirect by Mr. Karnavas, I believe that we can still finish this witness today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Scott, I thought you had one hour and 31 minutes left, unless I'm mistaken. You told us that you only needed one hour. So you don't need any additional hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, you were, I thought I was clear. I'm asking the Chamber for an additional hour above the time that I have remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. While I can sympathise with the Prosecution for wishing to spend additional time with this particular witness, I must confess that at times, I felt that he did not appropriately use his time. There were matters that were not terribly relevant, matters that were already established and nonetheless he went over them again and again and matters that are not necessarily relevant for this particular witness. Had the Prosecution been more efficient, I probably would be a little more generous that's number one. Number two, it's not a matter of whether we can finish this witness today. I have another witness who is very busy who can only be here this week. I cannot bring him back next week and I cannot bring him back some other point in time. He's been here since Friday. And I'm willing to reduce my time in that witness to make sure that he can finish this week so we can go back on schedule, on track, but I must object to the Prosecution having additional time. Now, if, for instance, the Prosecution were to make some sort of case as to exactly what were the areas, what are the areas that they need to go into specifically, it might help you and it might help me assess whether that additional time is warranted but thus far, all I've heard is they've reduced the scope of what they want to discuss and they need still an additional hour and I think we all have to manage our time. I also wish to point out that there were times when I wanted witnesses and one witness that still bothers me almost on a daily basis, it really gets under my skin, is the one ambassador that we had who was with the Mr. Vance and was with Mr. Owen taking all those notes, I was limited to 3 hours. I needed an additional day with that gentleman. I wasn't given any additional time. And that witness was here for only four days. This gentleman has been here five, he's going to be here another session, I think that's sufficient. There comes a point in time when we all need to manage our time as best as we can and I think we're doing that on this side and while I sympathise with the Prosecution, they haven't made a case yet that would warrant reconsideration of the time that you've provided to them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems there's no interpretation into English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The colleague said that the translation is on the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now, the English channel?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you receiving the interpretation into the B/C/S? I first greeted everyone in the courtroom and then I proceeded to say the following. The Petkovic Defence has a lot of understanding for the needs of all of the parties in these proceedings. We understand that everybody must be given sufficient time to hear the witnesses and this should also be beneficial to the Chamber. In that sense, we backed every application by the OTP to be granted more time for their own witnesses. We also believe they should be granted as much time as they can use for cross-examining Defence witnesses. However, the Petkovic Defence must in this case oppose the application by the Prosecution to be granted another hour for the present witness because the Prosecutor explains their application by their understanding of the other cross-examinations by the other Defences which is an approach that I consider to be entirely impermissible. We do not think it should be an established practice here that the cross-examinations by the other Defence teams should be seen as the same thing as the examination in chief by whichever Defence calls the witness. Should the OTP application be admitted, however, the Petkovic Defence will be requiring additional time to hear the witness on some circumstances that the Prosecutor has raised on their cross-examination of the witness as well as additional documents that they have introduced. The circumstances in these documents are of exceptional importance to the Petkovic Defence and we must shed light on them, therefore, we shall be applying for additional time to examine Mr. Akmadzic should this application by the Prosecution be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, you will have the floor in a minute. Mr. Scott, you're asking for an additional hour, again we're going to spend an hour on the issue but never mind. Mr. Scott, what are the topics that you would like to deal with in this additional hour? Which are the documents that you wanted to use?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a few clean-up items from yesterday including one additional document about the events in January of 1993. That was the last topic we were on yesterday. There was an important meeting that this witness was directly involved in at Citluk on the 29th of April, 1993, which I think was very important to put before the Chamber. The witness's previous testimony is short but nonetheless very important statement about the provision of military assistance and ammunition to the Muslims which has been raised in this courtroom -- by the Croat side which has been raised in this courtroom a number of times. The man -- the Defence spent a considerable amount of time on a man named Fikret Abdic which under the circumstances I would only take only in the most brief way but I think cannot be given the total amount -- given the amount of time spent by the Defence, I don't think I can completely leave this topic ignored. There are a number of different additional documents about Mr. Akmadzic's role in various meetings and events. And finally, there are about five or six parts of presidential transcripts to put to the witness in which he was directly involved. And he was a participant in those meetings, Your Honour. With respect, with a brief response to Ms. Alaburic, whatever issues she may feel that she needs to raise as with -- as relates to her client, Mr. Petkovic, I don't anticipate any additional issues in today's examination at all, as far as I can recall, involving Mr. Petkovic. And so to that extent, I mean to the extent that Ms. Alaburic has any issues or puts any requests before the Chamber about that, that stands completely independent of whether the Chamber grants the additional time or not because I don't expect to touch upon, I don't recall in looking through my notes again, my folders again, any involvement by Mr. Petkovic in any of the material that I would cover this morning. So that matter stands independent of this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'll take the lead from your learned brother, Judge Trechsel, I think Your Honours have heard enough on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following deliberations, the Trial Chamber decides to add 30 minutes to the remaining time, so you will have two hours, Mr. Scott, in order to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. I'll do my best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have the witness brought in. Yes, Ms. Alaburic, we'll see depending on the answers provided by the witness whether the Trial Chamber, I, personally, I have my own opinion, but whether the Trial Chamber will grant you additional time or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given the time that was granted for my cross-examination, there was something -- it was one of the things that gave rise to Mr. Scott's request then you partially granted that request, I will be asking for another five minutes and I will explain what the three topics are in which I would like to hear this witness; however, I think it might be a good idea for us to deal with this at the end of this witness's cross-examination so that then we can see what we do about it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry you had to wait for 20 minutes. I we had to deal with a point of procedure. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Once again, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Sir, our time is very limited today and everyone wants to get you back home hopefully at the end of the day depending on the travel schedule. So I'll appreciate if we can both move as efficiently as possible, I'll try and if you try to give your concise answers, that would be helpful. Sir, you've repeatedly stated -- just to bring us back up to speed from the last few days, you've repeatedly told us, if I understand your testimony correctly, that the HVO was considered an integral part of the armed forces of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the Supreme Command of the BiH Presidency in principle; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as the President Judge Antonetti correctly said yesterday at page 71, in the military there has to be one Supreme Commander and then there is a hierarchy in the chain of command and I take it you would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was a bit peculiar if the Supreme Command is the Presidency then it's 7, or rather, during the war, 7 plus 3 equals 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And sir, I think you would agree with me that at no time between April of 1992, which was the beginning point for most of the questions that I've been putting to you, and approximately January of 1994, there was no time during that period that Mate Boban was a member of the BiH Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so, sir, if the HVO was an integral part of the armed forces of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the Supreme Command of the BiH Presidency, in principle, it was not then under the command of Mate Boban; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if, as you've told us, the HVO was an integral part of the armed forces of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if the Supreme Command of those armed forces was in the BiH Presidency, then it was not -- it could not be the case, could it, that Mr. Boban was the Supreme Commander of those forces.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban could not have been the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, he could have been the commander of one of their segments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, in what way -- are you suggesting that Mr. Boban, then, himself in turn, would be subject to the Supreme Command of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina were under the Supreme Command of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a civilian body, the Supreme Command as head of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, going back to, again, what President Antonetti said yesterday, there had been one Supreme Commander. I put to you, sir, that the HVO couldn't have two Supreme Commanders. It couldn't be one and the same time that the Supreme Commander was the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and at the same time that Mate Boban was the Supreme Commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday when the Chamber asked that the Presidency as the Supreme Commander of the armed forces was one thing and the other thing was the joint command of all three components making up the BH army; one was the BH army, and the other was the HVO. I explained to the Trial Chamber yesterday that even in the joint command there could have been a number of people, five, seven, three, whatever, but I really don't know much about that, how many people exactly but the joint command could possibly have more people in the -- in that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. If you can please look at Exhibit P 01312, which should be in the second binder, please. P 01312. While you're looking for that, sir, at the same time, for the record I will say that this appears to be a letter or communication by Bruno Stojic dated the 26th of January, 1993, touching on the issues that we discussed yesterday in connection with the decision issued on the 15th of January, 1993, for the subordination or relocation of certain forces. 1312. All right. Sir, if you will look at the last page of that document, in the paragraph, the last paragraph over the name of Mr. Stojic. About halfway through that paragraph, in response to a letter that we looked at yesterday by Mr. Halilovic, Mr. Stojic says, "For our part, we are unconditionally prepared to carry out the order of our Supreme Commander, Mr. Boban." So again I ask you sir, this could not be correct, could it if in fact the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the Supreme Commander, collectively the Supreme Commander of the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we must see who we are, Mr. Bruno Stojic. We are certainly the HVO. A segment of the HVO according to his opinion here is Mr. Boban, meaning Mr. Boban is the civilian Supreme Commander of the HVO, according to what we are looking at here. But not of all the armed forces such as the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So I put it to you again, sir, that subject to -- consistent with the testimony you've given so far, are you suggesting, then, that if the HVO was one integral part of the armed forces of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and if you say, if you say that Mr. Boban was the Commander in Chief of one particular segment, are you telling this Chamber then that Mr. Boban was subject to and reported to the BiH Presidency as the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. Boban was submitting reports to the BH Presidency but I know that the BH Presidency had information about the functioning of the HVO as a segment of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention back to the previous page or the previous paragraph above the one that I've been looking at. In the English version it is the bottom of page 3. Mr. Stojic also makes this statement, "I am head of the Defence department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna" and in line with the questions I've been putting to you in the last few moments, do you agree that there is no basis whatsoever to suggest that during this time from approximately the middle of 1992 to January 1994, Mr. Stojic as the head of the Herceg-Bosna Defence department was reporting to or taking direction from the BiH Presidency as the Supreme Commander, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that at the time that we were at the negotiations and the BH Presidency was meeting abroad we were exchanging whatever information was available but there was no reporting in writing, as such. We would reach any agreements at the meetings of the Presidency. Therefore, I am unable to answer your last question with any degree of precision whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you inform this Chamber of any occasion that you recall concerning a meeting of the BiH Presidency, and in the past week or so we've looked at a number of the minutes of those meetings, can you recall a single meeting where Bruno Stojic directly or indirectly gave a report about the workings of his department to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But what I can say is this: By virtue, his position at the time, Bruno Stojic was not directly in touch with the BH Presidency. There were segments between him and the BH Presidency that he might have reported to, for example, the Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn next, please, to Exhibit P -- in the first binder, P 00042 [Realtime transcript read in error "P 000402"]. It should be the first document in the first binder. 42, sorry, the transcript says 402, if I misspoke, I'm sorry. P 00042. Exhibit 42. Sir, I just want to touch briefly again and to conclude on this particular topic that we've discussed building on some of your evidence you gave yesterday. Isn't it correct, sir, that throughout the period from even the middle of 1991 and continuing until late 1992, there were extensive division of views and dissent among even the leadership of the HDZ-BiH which was not finally overcome until November 1992 and I put it to you, sir, by which time all or most of the moderates of that party including Mr. Kljuic, Mr. Brkic and others had left the party or had been thrown out of the party or had been marginalised; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at Exhibit P 00042, a record of a meeting of the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ-BiH in the Travnik region on the 21st of, July, 1991, and I direct your attention in particular to paragraph number 5. In that paragraph, it says, "If President Stjepan Kljuic is unable to leave the HDZ-BiH Presidency because of his position as a member of the BiH Presidency," look at that, I next direct your attention to -- and I'll put a question to you to paragraph numbered 13 which reports among other things "HDZ deputies," I take it in the BiH assembly in the -- in reference to the previous sentence, "had become puppets of the SDA policies"; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to raise an objection at this point. If you look at number five, this is a clever way of trying to piece together something to fit the Prosecution's aims. If you look at paragraph 5, "Because of his position as a member," it goes, "it is recommended that the sessions be presided over by the other vice-presidents or another authorised member of the Presidency." What does that mean? Maybe he has functions and he cannot attend the meeting. Not because of his political views which is what the Prosecution is suggesting. So I would object to this first and foremost; and secondly, what does this have to do with the price of eggs in China. Why is this relevant? Or tea. I just don't see what the relevance is. He's asked for 30 additional minutes or an hour and now we're wasting our time on this. Why is this relevant with this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in response, number one, I don't have time to put all -- as again, I don't have time to put all the documents in front of this witness to demonstrate this point. I can ask the witness, I think, it would be -- I would be surprised if it would be disputed in this courtroom at this point that there was a significant difference of views between Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Boban, Mr. Kostroman and others. I think that seems to be pretty well known in the courtroom at this particular point in time. Secondly, Your Honour, I think the directly and highly relevant because there are continued -- it's the Prosecution case that there are continued references in the documentation and continued pretense that the HDZ spoke for all Croats, spoke for all parts of that party and that in fact, the HDZ in its earlier period included a wide range of opinions and that the party that existed and was most relevant at the end of 1992 leads us into the core events of this indictment. That HDZ at the end of 1992 was a substantially different HDZ than the one that started in 1990 and 1991. And if the Defence says that's not disputed, then we'll take that as an established fact and go forward. If it is disputed then the Prosecution should be allowed to put its case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as in any political party, there are divergent opinions. You can see that now going on in the elections in the United States, can you see in Croatia today with the various parties or in Bosnia. That is not in dispute. That's -- that's common the world over. Number one. Number two, Kljuic resigned, let's be clear on that. He resigned. He can put the question to him whether he resigned or whether he was forced out. Kljuic resigned. That's a fact that has been established in this courtroom. Now, whether he came under pressure, whether he was being criticised and resigned, it doesn't matter. He resigned. But what does this have to do -- are we prosecuting HDZ, is this what this case is about? Let us focus on the case, Your Honours. I truly plead with you to keep this focus on what is at stake. Otherwise we are prosecuting everything. And then we have to defend everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour that's simply not true and if it's -- again, I invite Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed because the Chamber is of the view that this has a relevance with regard to the joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Kljuic, according to the Prosecution, left the leadership of the HDZ, that's the Prosecution case so the Prosecution can confront the witness with that. You may proceed with your question, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Akmadzic, it may be that counsel's partly right that I may not have picked perhaps the very best document of the various dozens of documents on this point to put in front of you, but you know, don't you, that even by mid-1991 by the fall 1991, by the time of a very important meeting in Zagreb on the 27th of December, 1991, there was a substantial division of views in the HDZ-BiH personified if you will, at that time, the division of the conflict between Mr. Boban and the people like Mr. Boban and Mr. Kordic on one hand and people like Mr. Kljuic on the other; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like us to deal with this subject once and for all and could I please not answer questions on this topic any longer. The HDZ won the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina with the vast majority and to this day, the HDZ is in power in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the segment that relates to the Croatian people. The HDZ was not always unanimous and we never considered that to be a smart thing or a good thing. In socialism, we used to call that single-mindedness and we decided to fight against that at all levels and among all three peoples. That is to say that in 1990, and further on when we carried out elections and when we had a change of government, we said that we had a democratic government in which all people had the right to present their own views. At this point in time, I disagree with the Prosecutor on the following. Namely, he considers Mr. Kljuic and some others to be moderates and then he probably considers others to be immoderates or extremists or whatever. I cannot agree with that at all because I first and foremost do not think that Mr. Kljuic is all that moderate. The most moderate almost among all of them was myself, that is what was generally believed and therefore please respect my views. These views were expressed democratically. Mr. Kljuic resigned because he did not agree with the majority, that is his right and that is a possibility that he had. I agree that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Chamber is going to grant me more time, I'm going to cut you off and go on. You've stated your position. I would like for you to look at P 00743. P 00743 which should be in the second binder. 743. Sir, this is the record of a meeting of the HDZ-BiH second general assembly held in Mostar on the 14th of November, 1992. There are actually a large number of points raised in this document but time does not allow us to go through many of them. In the first page, I will just direct your attention ever so briefly to item number 3 indicating the so-called distinguished guest from the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Susak and Mr. Pasalic, Mr. Vukjevic, Perica Juric. The distinguished guest from BiH and BiH organs, number 5, Mile Akmadzic, Miro Lasic, Franjo Boras and others including Jadranko Prlic. Stopping briefly on item number 7, it said it began with a salute with the home land by striking up the anthem. And with my apologies I may say it, Lijepa Nasa. That is the national anthem of the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is the anthem of the Croatian people, that the Croatian state took as its own; however, the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina also sing that anthem. While I'm on the subject, allow me to tell you that there are also two flags that are very similar, one is the flag of the Republic of Croatia and the other one is of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Hercegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're right, sir, the flags are very, very similar. If I can ask you then to go to specifically to item number 22 in the English version, it is the bottom of page 5. To touch on and confirm by documentation something we discussed yesterday, it's correct, sir, that it was at this meeting, as reflected in item 22, that Mate Boban was elected president of the HDZ-BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then in item 23, several vice-presidents were elected at the proposition of Mate Boban: You; Mr. Dario Kordic; Mr. Jadranko Topic, who was the HVO mayor or president of Mostar; and Mr. Ivo Zivkovic. And the four of you were put forward if you will nominated by Mr. Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect. We were proposed and elected by the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When it says, "At the proposition of Mate Boban ..." you're saying that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proposition and election is not one and the same thing. I am a linguist, at least I know about that. They were elected by the HDZ and the parliament and it's not one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps you misheard me or there was a translation difference, sir. The point, the question that I put to you was not who voted but at -- but by who you were proposed or nominated and I take it, then, you agree with me that you were nominated by Mr. Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. We've already discussed that in this courtroom that nomination or, rather, appointment and election is not one and the same thing. The word used here is "elected," "izabrani."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In item 24 similarly at the proposition of Mate Boban, 40 people were elected to the BiH central board and do I take it that the central board was like the principal or executive board of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot discuss the party here and now. We don't have the Statute of the party before us so we cannot see how elections take place in accordance with the Statute of the party. We discussed some other matters yesterday and we said that the rules of procedure of the Presidency were somewhat different in respect of what we had discussed earlier on or rather if you look at what it was that I claimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, excuse me. Witness, I would like to come back to the issue of nominations and elections. Let's have a look at paragraph 23 where it mentions the election of the vice-president and following the interpretation into French, I heard -- that's what I heard at the proposition of Mate Boban, those persons were elected. Elected, fine. But what about that proposition? You were nominated by Mr. Boban or were you proposed by Mr. Boban to be part of a list that comprised more than four people? In other words, Mr. Boban proposed four persons, nominated four persons and those four persons were elected or did he propose more persons, five, six or ten persons, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember. I think that Mr. Boban proposed these five persons who were indeed elected and I think there were other proposals made by other members of the party but at this point, I cannot confirm that or deny it. The fact remains that Mr. Boban made the proposal and that all the members who were there as delegates elected this leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. The assembly had the authority to accept or refuse those persons; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All four persons could have been refused, also the election of Mate Boban and the president could have been refused. The assembly is the top body of the party; was then, is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we could next go to Exhibit P 02142 which should be in the second binder, please. P 02142. Sir, this is a report concerning a meeting in Citluk on the 29th of April, 1993, of the Presidency apparently of -- well, a number of people. It's indicated at the top of the page the Presidency, the government of the HZ HB, HVO, et cetera. During -- about halfway down the first page, you're indicated as being present, Mr. Mile Akmadzic. Down below your name, several items down, past the what we might call the bulleted items, there is a statement attributed under your section, if you will, of the record, you say, "Suggested officially disputing the mandate of Mr. A. Izetbegovic in the capacity of president (of 2 November 1992)." Now, sir, are we to take it from that, the way I would read it and I'm giving you the chance, of course, to disagree with me, but is it correct then that up to that point in time since you're suggesting this is something to be done, that up until that point in time, Mr. Izetbegovic's capacity as president had not been "officially disputed"?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed that yesterday. Mr. Izetbegovic's Presidency was disputed as of the 20th of December, 1992. For the sake of compromise, he was accepted after that because he was a member of the Presidency and he led the majority people of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the negotiations. We cannot disregard that fact but as president of the Presidency, we challenged him, disputed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Prior to the Citluk meeting on the 29th April, 1993, had the HDZ leadership, Mr. Boban, yourself, Mr. Kordic, others, had any of you -- had the party "officially disputed" Mr. Izetbegovic's mandate as president? Prior to the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please separate the party from the state now although its representatives are in the state government. The mandate of Mr. Izetbegovic was disputed by members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the ranks of the Croatian people, that is to say, state officials. The party can only have a consultative link in that respect, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please go to Exhibit P 10482 in the third binder, please. P 10482. Sir, this is a report of a interview that it indicates you gave on the 4th of May, 1993, to a Zagreb daily publication called Vecernji List. Excuse me if I mispronounce it but I believe that's close. It indicates that you gave an interview which was then published in this Zagreb newspaper on the 4th of May, 1993, a few days after the Citluk meeting on the 29th of April. In the third paragraph of that it attributes the statement to you, "He says that he does not rule out the Croatian members of the government based in the southern town of Mostar proclaiming themselves government of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is that an accurate report of the statement of the interview you gave on the 4th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find what you read out to me now, but I can confirm the following: I did not authorise this interview which would be normal. Secondly, the meetings you referred to just now -- well, I think the dates are not correct. And I don't know whether this matters altogether. I would not look at this newspaper interview, this is not an official paper. I did not authorise this and I cannot remember now what it was that I had said in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by authorise, sir. Did you give an interview sometime around the 4th of May, 1993, or not? Let's start with that and then we'll go forward. Did you give an interview around this time or did this Zagreb newspaper just completely make this up?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me explain what I mean by the word "authorisation." When one gives an interview ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you give an interview?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Probably -- I can't remember. I gave many interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the question from Mr. Scott "I don't know what you mean by authorise, sir." So now he's trying to give an explanation of what he means by authorise. You can see that. Of course Mr. Scott goes on with his question ending with a rather sarcastic note but nonetheless, he begins by saying, "I don't know what you mean by authorise." So now the gentleman is trying to explain what he means by authorise. Now he can't have it both ways. He can't ask a question and then slap him down when he tries to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not slapping down, Your Honour. As Mr. Karnavas likes to say, it's trying to proceed step by step. I rephrased, I gave priority to establishing the first point first and that is, one, was there an interview; if we can establish that there was an interview, then we can talk about whether it was authorised or not and that's all that was, Your Honour. There's no reason to take time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you say you don't recall giving an interview, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I said that I gave a great many interviews. As for this specific interview, I do not remember it. However, I'm not claiming that I did not give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your position around this time in May -- late April, early May 1993, was it your position that -- is it something that you were considering that the Croat members of the government based in the southern town of Mostar might proclaim themselves the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interject here for a second. I'm told by my colleague who reads Croatian, I don't, that when you compare the text what has been translated and when you compare it to the actual document, they're not the same. And that this text here that we have in our hands is not the interview or this article from this newspaper. One is not connected to the other. It might be a montage, it might be an interpretation, but this is -- this document here which is in Croatian which is from the newspaper itself has not been interpreted. That's what I am told. So perhaps that may be the reason -- so we have an agency interpreting what was said and that may be the cause of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, that had not escaped me. The first document is a document from the AFP which is a French agency so this is already a translation. Secondly, we have an article with the witness's picture. Maybe you should show the article to the witness. I'm looking at the article and it seems to me that there are questions and answers. The question is in black and the answer in grey. You have a B/C/S speaking assistant, maybe she can show you where is the question that is then mentioned by AFP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't have that assistance in the courtroom, Your Honour, if the Chamber wants me to do that, I will pursue it outside the courtroom. The question is -- I see that the witness has the article. He has a larger version, a much larger version, fold-out version of the article which hopefully makes it more legible. Your Honour, I would like Mr. Karnavas -- unfortunately, I can't claim to be able to read the original document; I can only stand here and say that this is the translation that I was given of the document. It may be there is a part of the document, a part of the interview that has been republished, and if the witness can look at the original interview in the item which gives -- includes his picture, if you recognise the picture of a bit younger man, as we all were 15 years ago, but I can't read, Your Honour, the document either. So unless the witness can assist us, we will have to get somebody from outside the courtroom to assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe you could come back to that issue after the break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will do that. Let me just have a moment. Thank you, Mr. President, we'll try to sort that out. Although I must say, if the witness says he doesn't deny the interview but he doesn't specifically remember it, I'm not sure how much it helps us, frankly, and I would just simply put the questions to him that the -- the outstanding question that I had in fact put to him whether he recalls the interview or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it, nonetheless, his position around this time, the end April 1993, early May 1993 that the Croatian members of the government based in the southern town of Mostar might or were considering proclaiming themselves the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe the witness can still answer that question with or without the interview. Was that your position at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we please leave the newspapers aside and maybe I can give you my position. I didn't think then, nor indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly what I just said. If you don't remember the particular interview then just answer my question which you were just about to do. So we both said the same thing. So was that your position at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't believe then nor do I believe now that we Croats could have set up the BH government on our own. That is nonsense. If that is what the papers say, then this is a misinterpretation of my words. I must add this too --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your position at the time, sir, that it's also reported in this article but whether you remember it or not I will just put the proposition to you. Do you remember holding this position at the time that as of that same period of time, Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer exists as a legal entity as it no longer controls all of its territory even though it is recognised by the international community? Was that your position at this time?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't my position either. In this courtroom, everybody should know what my position was by now. The Presidency given its function did not have full legitimacy, control over the territory is a different matter altogether. You can have a country that is occupied but still an internationally recognised country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your position that Bosnia and Herzegovina as of April and May 1993, no longer existed as a legal entity?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered. He just answered the question. Now we can do this over and over again and this is why I'm a little bit upset with the Trial Chamber this morning for granting additional time without first allowing him to exhaust the present time that he was given. He's abusing your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm trying to get a straight answer. What the witness said was - and it's on the page in front of us - he came back and answered in terms of the legitimacy of the Presidency. My question was a different one and it's not limited just to the issue of the Presidency. I'm putting what is reported -- what is reported to be a statement by this man which said, at the time, Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer exists as a legal entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm asking him whether he confirms that position or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You've indicated that the Prosecutor, who does not read B/C/S or does not read Croatian, should take the time to read it over the break. We put our case that this is either an interpretation of an interview or simply a montage. Now, until that is established, I think it's highly improper for the gentleman to stand here and say, "This was your position." He can ask him the question, which he has done. But to say that we have this interview here and this is what he held back then and I'm putting it to him now, we don't know that. This is -- yes, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I haven't heard the Prosecutor put it to him that it was his position but asking him an almost open question whether -- whether, whether it was his position or not, independent of the article. And the witness himself says let's forget about the article and speak about the issues. I thought this was what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But then he -- then Mr. Scott goes back into the article. He can ask those questions, what were your positions on this and this and this and this, irrespective of what the article says, but then to ground the question and say, well, this is what was in the article and that's what I heard; so he's having it both ways. He can put only his -- he can put his case squarely and fairly to the witness all day long; I will not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, you're exactly right. I didn't have to put this document even into evidence. I can have it in front of me as a basis for putting questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly where you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You did refer to the statement, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will restate it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask you again. Was it your position in April-May 1993, was it your position that Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist at that time as a legal entity?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of Bosnia-Herzegovina existed as a state. As for legal or legal, I think lawyers should shed light on that, because I don't know what that means. Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time you specified existed as an international entity and as a state, quite regardless of any internal problems that it may or may not have been facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you, sir, and a majority of the Croatian members of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina left Sarajevo as of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, our proposal was for the government to move out of Sarajevo as well as the Presidency. Sarajevo was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question what the proposal was. My question was had you, had you and a majority of the Croat members in fact moved out of Sarajevo as of December 1992. That's my question. Please answer that question. Yes or no, had you moved out of Sarajevo as of December 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members were leaving at various points in time. They didn't all leave in December 1992 and they would then return to Sarajevo. And then they met again. You have transcripts showing me our Presidency meetings both in Sarajevo and outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... as of December 1992 and except for perhaps coming back to Sarajevo on some specific occasions you remained out of Sarajevo through the balance of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, back in 1992, after Christmas, between Christmas and New Year's Eve actually, on or about the 28th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that's not my question --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was your question, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I said, sir, did you leave Sarajevo as of December of 1992 and except for going back on some limited occasions, you remained out of Sarajevo. You didn't live there. You didn't stay there anymore except for perhaps, perhaps coming back on some occasions; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no, I'm sorry. I can't say because I was off to the Geneva negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't know where you lived in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, my flat in Sarajevo had been looted and I was unable to go back to Sarajevo, but I did go to all the rounds of negotiations to the meetings and I took part in negotiations abroad. My flat was all looted and I had absolutely no access to it. I want to make that perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes, you were not in Sarajevo except on some occasions after December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be your conclusion. Draw any conclusion that you like, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you touched on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness, I'm a bit frustrated because the Prosecutor legitimately asked you questions that can be answered by yes or no. There may always be explanations but you have always avoided answering the question and started giving explanations and this makes us lose a lot of time. It is a simple question that it cannot be seen that it could not be answered by yes or no and you have not been able to show why it could not be answered by yes or no. So I would ask you to comply with your duty as a witness to answer questions that can be answered yes or no by yes and no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, with all due respect, some questions are rather tricky. If he says yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I know that, Mr. Karnavas. This question is not one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is where and here is where I fundamentally disagree with you and perhaps because you may not have listened or picked up on what he was trying to say at a moment ago. If he's out on official duties and negotiations, so the answer is yes. But for the Prosecution's purposes, he's abandoned Sarajevo. Now, I cannot let you as the Judge draw a conclusion that he left Sarajevo when in fact he was on official duty. He was trying to give an explanation and I do think that he's entitled to that. He's not here as a trained seal to say yes or no and I cannot explain. In this instance, he was trying to say exactly the circumstance under which he left and if he's on official duty, it's rather different than saying he's abandoned the city. That's what he was trying to do. And I thought that had he been given some leeway, he might have been able to answer and get to the question -- and I do disagree with you that when you say he is never or he is not answering the questions. He's trying. Maybe he's not doing it our way but he is making an attempt to be fair so you can make and draw the proper conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it is you who have drawn a conclusion that he had abandoned Sarajevo. I did not take this conclusion. And it's not what I think. I find this is a typical case where the witness answers yes or no and in redirect, you solicit the explanation and you put it in the light which is the right light in the view of the Defence. That's how I understand the rules of the games and I think we should all try to abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying but -- I will just -- I will sit down because I think that -- I don't want to get into polemics with the Trial Chamber. I do believe that the gentleman was attempting to answer the question. I'm trying -- I don't want you to draw the wrong conclusion hence why I said perhaps had he been given the opportunity to explain why he's not there. And if you're going to say -- if the burden is going to be on redirect then I'm going to have be spending a lot of my time on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we must say, the Petkovic Defence, with the greatest respect we do support Mr. Karnavas on this. It wasn't a simple yes or no question and in fact if we look at the question at page 30, lines 15 to 18, it's not put in an absolutely simple form. There are in fact two or three very slightly differently -expressed questions there and to ask somebody to say: Did you live somewhere except for leaving going back on some limited occasions? We all live our lives like that and drawing the line between living permanently in a place and you're bound to go out of the place from time to time and being away for longer, it's not simple yes or no and the chances of a simple yes or no being the appropriate answer would be significantly enhanced if the question were put in one single, simple form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it is a very clear problem nothing to do with respect for one or the other. We have an article in B/C/S. We don't know its contents because it has not been translated. We have a dispatch from the French agency, press agency AFP which seems to relate totally to your interview or your statement. We don't know exactly what it is, but in reference to the article and the AFP dispatch seems to say that you said that Bosnia and Herzegovina no longer existed as an entity and the last paragraph of the dispatch says that you continued to act as a prime minister although the majority of the Croat members in the government had left Sarajevo in December. So this is what the dispatch conveys and the Prosecutor seems to rely on this dispatch because he doesn't know exactly what there is in the article itself. In December, you were the prime minister. A prime minister has ministers as work sessions, meetings. In December, did you keep meeting with the other ministers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where did you, in Sarajevo or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Sarajevo in the government's offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said your flat was looted. When you would go back to Sarajevo, where would you stay? Did you have another apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would go back the same day and UNPROFOR helped with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if you had work meetings at the government level, you would go back with the UNPROFOR -- or you would go to Sarajevo with the UNPROFOR, that's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I think I sorted out the problem so we may continue. Yes, you had a follow-up question, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on the President's question, sir. When you said you would go back the same day, where would you go back to?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would first go back to Herzegovina which is where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drinovci, the place called Drinovci. My brother owns a house there and that's where I would go. My family was there, my wife and my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To assist the courtroom for those of us who may not be particularly familiar with that location, I admit that I'm not, where was that located in reference to Mostar, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance from Mostar is about 50 or 60 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then when you said that you would go to attend some meetings in Sarajevo with at least on some occasions with the assistance of UNPROFOR, approximately how many times in 1993 did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go to important meetings, especially the Presidency meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the important meetings, how many times did you go, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five or six. I can't be more specific, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving to another topic then. The -- you also touched upon in your earlier questioning by Mr. Karnavas and perhaps others the provision of military assistance, ammunition, equipment, what have you, from the Croat side to the Muslims and it's correct, sir, is it not, that that happened -- there were certainly times when the Croat side whether that be people in Grude or people in Zagreb provided aid or -- military aid or assistance to the Muslim side but that was during -- those were during times -- that assistance was given during times when there was not a war going on between the Croats and the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really unable to distinguish. I'm unable to confirm and I'm unable to deny. What's more, I think there were always some clashes or, rather, it -- just some didn't escalate or they escalated to a greater or lesser extent. There were ongoing clashes and the aid was always on its way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Kordic case at page 20480 to 481 on the 6th of June, 2000, you testified under oath as follows: "As for the ammunition which the Muslims received or did not receive from Croats, it depended on the political situation so that it is possible when the political relations were better, then it could have happened; but when the conflicts escalated, then it was prevented so the whole situation was a zigzag situation." That's the testimony you gave in the Kordic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is roughly what I've been saying now. It's very difficult to repeat myself word for word because this was, after all, eight years ago. I think the gist remains the same then as now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, we don't have time to discuss this man at any length but perhaps it will suffice for now, and I say "for now." Concerning this man Fikret Abdic, he was and is a convicted war criminal; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that in the papers. I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He was convicted in July 2002 and sentenced to 20 years imprisonment for the crimes involving camps and detention centres which were operated under his leadership. He was convicted for inhumane treatment of prisoners and civilians including torture and forced labour. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I wasn't there. I did read in the papers at the time that Mr. Fikret Abdic was convicted of some crimes or other, but I can't tell you more about something that went on in Bihac or Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the papers that you read, you recall reading it being reported that the sentencing judge said that the prisoners who were tortured the most were Abdic's political opponents?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, to Exhibit P 10468 which should be in the third binder, binder number three. P 10468. Sir, this is a publication of an interview in the Washington Post on the 16th of February, 1993. And let me just read a couple of portions to you and then I'll put a couple of questions to you. The article says starting at the beginning of the article, "Having a conversation with Mile Akmadzic, the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is like talking to three different people. Sometimes he speaks as an official of a sovereign government and lays out its position on civil war and peace. Sometimes he speaks in the voice of a Croat nationalist and rails against the government's stands and against the Serbs and the Muslims." The next paragraph purporting to quote you, "'Sometimes I speak personally,' he said during an interview last week. 'So it can be confusing.'" Now, is that a fair statement, whether you recall, again, the exact interview or not, would you consider that to be an accurate statement of your three different, and I don't mean in any disrespect, sir, your three different personalities or wearing your three different hats? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say three different hats. I would say three different features or something like that. But not hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The second page of the article about halfway -- a little above halfway down the page, this statement is attributed to you, "Akmadzic, predictably, is of three minds regarding Vance-Owen," and I pause to indicate this is 16 February 1993, "Akmadzic, predictably, is of three minds regarding Vance-Owen. 'The government will not accept it as proposed,' he says, 'speaking as prime minister.'" So you knew, sir, as this goes back to what we were talking about yesterday, you knew that even by February, let alone the 15th of January, even by February, the government, the BiH government would not accept and had not accepted the Vance-Owen Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The negotiations were in progress at the time and they were difficult negotiations. When we say the government here, it's not what it means, you know that when in America they say "government" they mean something else and this means Presidency. This means negotiators on behalf of the Presidency. That was my opinion because the negotiations were tough going. Eventually the negotiations were successful, well, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I look at the clock, it may be a couple of minutes early but I'm about to start a new topic. This might be a place to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please look at this same document because the last paragraph seems important to me. Indeed, you're saying things here that may be relevant. Have you seen the last paragraph on page 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. May I now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling the reporter that you are a Bosnian at heart, that you belong to the Croat people but not to the state of Croatia. Is that what you said? You say this to a newspaper that is indeed very famous, the Washington Post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say that. Yes. Yes. I did say that. I can't remember. It was a long time ago but I think that's what I said that I was a Bosnian, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Not a Bosnian as in a Bosniak. Not the way we defined it back in Washington because there were two different terms being used: From Bosnia, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and on the other hand, a Bosniak as an ethnicity which is what the Muslims chose to term themselves at the time. But there was no such thing at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the time has come for the break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have located the full translation of the previous article. That is P 10 -- well, now I have two different numbers, I'm afraid. Is it P 10482 or 483? 482. 10482.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you still have the large version of the Croatian language original and then you should have before you -- and I understand by now that you read at least a fair amount of English so you can refer to either one that assists you the most. If I can refer your attention to either the bottom of page 8 -- excuse me, the bottom of page 1, my apologies, the bottom of page 1 of the English version or in the original language version toward the end of -- if you start under your picture and there is what might be called a -- there is a dot and then a dash and after the dash it says, "Za" -- it appears to say "Za." And at the end of that same paragraph, it says this, "I left Sarajevo before the New Year's Day with an authorisation of the government to take part in the Geneva talks on the internal organisation of BiH. I did not return to Sarajevo after that." Now do you agree with that? Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in Sarajevo on the 20th January attending negotiations with Vance and Owen and attending the sessions of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And going to page 2 of the English translation and to -- I think again if you can look in your article if you like, the third -- the fourth dot, if you will, on that left-hand column. There is one, two, three, four toward the bottom of that first left column, you also see this language which is at the bottom of page 2 of the English version, "Unfortunately, I rarely have contacts with members of the government in Sarajevo. My office phone is switched off. The connections are very bad so I can say that I am not in contact whatsoever with the Muslim members of the government. We, Croat members of the government, are all outside of Sarajevo but one. We have regular meetings and consultations so we are in a way involved in activities which may relate to both the BiH government and the HVO." Is that the information that you provided to the Vecernji List on the 4th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I next ask you, please, to look at P 10472 which again should be in the third binder. P 10472. Sir, this appears to be another interview or article involving or touching upon you, dated the 27th of August, 1993. In the -- I believe, fifth paragraph of the article, it says this, and the article is written, again, the 27th of August, 1993, so I suggest to you that when it refers to January, it is referring to January 1993. "In January, Akmadzic travelled to Geneva with the Bosnian delegation but transferred when he got there to the Croat delegation led by Bosnian Croat leader Mate Boban. He has since been based either in the Croatian capital Zagreb or in Grude, a Croat stronghold in southwestern Bosnia and has made only brief trips to Sarajevo." Are those statements accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct and as you can see, I did not leave Sarajevo in January, I went to Geneva. I went on the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What is inaccurate here is that I was not stationed either in Zagreb or Grude. I spent most of my time at the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next ask you to go to Exhibit P 10473, also in the third binder. It should be pretty close to the -- should be the next document than the one you're looking at now, 10473, which appears to be another article in the Washington Post dated the 24th of December, 1993. Directing your attention to the English version and if you want to find it elsewhere you may, on the second page of the article in the English translation and English -- I guess in this instance original since it's the Washington Post. It says, "Since Haris Silajdzic, the 48-year-old foreign minister, took over on October 25 as prime minister from his absentee Croat predecessor Mile Akmadzic, Sarajevo has become a new city." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot see that but I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it an accurate statement that you had been "the absentee Croat predecessor" to Mr. Silajdzic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absent in the sense that we've already discussed, yes, so absent and present too. Present from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You testified, sir, in the Kordic case that you were good friends with Mr. Mate Boban, that you had known him since childhood. Is it correct that you were good friends with Mr. Boban and had known him since childhood?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to read further on, everything that I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just answer my question, please, sir. Were you good friends with Mr. Boban. Had you known Mr. Boban since childhood?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him when we were children and then we did not see each other for 30 years or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you both born and raised in Grude?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the broader sense of the word, yes. Yes, in the municipality. However, we were not born on the same locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said in the Kordic case and, counsel, I'm referring to page 20409, 20409, on the 5th of June, 2000, "There were quite a few questions on which I did not entirely agree with Mr. Boban because I had also become part of the Sarajevo environment. However, we tried not to quarrel over those issues where we disagreed." Can you tell the Chamber any of the issues that you or questions that you can remember being in disagreement -- being in disagreement with Mr. Boban, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We disagreed because I liked Sarajevo. I practically became a Sarajevo local although I was born elsewhere, near the location of where Mr. Boban was born. Very often he would say that he didn't like Sarajevo. As a matter of fact, he never lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any disagreements with Mr. Boban on his policies or views in connection with Herceg-Bosna, its establishment and its operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, I was not present when Herceg-Bosna was established but I was more flexible and more moderate than Boban. He was a bit of a hardliner. I'm not trying to say that he was right or that I was right but we are different persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of an issue to use the word you used just now, an issue on where you considered Mr. Boban a hardliner where you disagreed with him?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that he was a hardliner. I said that that was his character as a person. I said that I was more moderate, so in that sense we did not always share the same views but we could cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said just now, sir, and I'm reading back to you line 24, page 43, "I said that that was his character as person; that is, that he was a hardliner." So can you give us again an example of an issue which you would attribute to Mr. Boban in his character as a hardliner with which you disagreed; or if you say you never disagreed with him, tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in negotiations, he advocated views when it would be hard for him to relent and when we had Mr. Izetbegovic's hard stance and on the other hand, Boban's hard stance, it was very hard to reach agreement. I advocated view points to the effect that there should be more compromise and there should be more true agreements and less politisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you disagree with Mr. Boban, for example, on territorial claims as to what territory comprised Herceg-Bosna or what territory should be given to the Croats as a result of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not talk about that. I did not want to talk about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, you're saying in all these peace negotiations in which you spent a great deal of time talking to us, Cutileiro, Vance-Owen, Owen-Stoltenberg, Washington Agreement, that in all those negotiations, you and Mr. Boban never had a conversation about territorial matters?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked in general terms not in detail. My understanding of your question was that you were interested in details. I was a major supporter of the Vance-Owen Plan. To this day I'm a supporter of this kind of a set up for Bosnia-Herzegovina and whether the territories will be bigger or smaller or what they will be like, that's a different question altogether. And the third question is that these territories did not only have a national character which is something that we've already established here, these territories, rather, in accordance with the Vance-Owen Plan or, rather, these provinces were the result of several different -- several different characteristics as we said, ethnic geographical, cultural, historical, all of these elements were supposed to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you on many occasions talked with both Boban and Tudjman about the territories claimed by Herceg-Bosna, about what borders should be established. You looked at maps with them. You discussed specific -- drafted specific language in proposed negotiation documents, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct, in fact, and following on from that that by the fall of 1992, when you became vice-president of the HDZ-BiH and prime minister, that from that time forward and into 1994, you were a right-hand man to both Tudjman and Boban in carrying out their programmes and policies; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, especially not for Tudjman. I never liked having an idol above me, let alone Tudjman who I always considered to be the president of a state that we were not negotiating in then. As for Boban, he was head of a delegation of which I was a member and only so when the internal establishment of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being discussed. Boban and I visited Canada as a state together. I have my passport here. I can show you where I travelled, where I was head of -- well, it's hard for me to say this but I was head of the delegation in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, throughout 1993 and into 1994 and perhaps thereafter, you worked hand-in-glove with Tudjman to carry out his directions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, please, to turn to Exhibit P 07480. P 07480 in binder number 2. P 07480. Sir, this is a record of a meeting with President Tudjman on the 5th of January, 1994. You will see on the first page that at least some of the persons participating are listed, Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Akmadzic, Mr. Mate Granic at the presidential residence on the 5th of January, 1994. And for present purposes, I would just like to turn your attention immediately, please, to page 15 and 16.
