At the bottom of page 15, the statement is attributed to the president "We have a meeting of the VONS," which has been indicated here as the National Security and Defence Council, "tomorrow." Do you agree, sir, because this has come up before, could you just quickly confirm to us that the VONS is accurately described here as the National Security and Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you recall how many times that you participated or attended any meeting of the VONS?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the top of page 16, after -- I'm going to the end of the transcript in terms of the ongoing talk about the negotiations, the peace negotiations, I think going to Bonn at this point in early January 1994. On the top of page 16 it says, Mile Akmadzic, "Mr. President, would it be better if I stayed here until Saturday, should I go on Saturday?" President: "No, no, you are going to Bonn. (So I should say here not go down there and not raise these questions.) Granic: "No, you should inform them about everything that happened. I think it is most important that you inform them about everything that happened. President: "Inform them but stay here. (You must say). Akmadzic: "I will inform Boban by telephone tomorrow. (Yes)." As I said to you a few moments ago, sir, isn't this in fact an illustration of one of many occasions where, as I said, you worked hand-in-glove with President Tudjman even taking specific direction from him as to where you should go or not go?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer. Could other microphones please be switched off. There is a lot of background nose, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not answer but you asked me for an explanation with regard to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you: Isn't it correct, sir, that this illustrates you working very closely with Mr. Tudjman and to the point of taking direction from him as to what you should do and where you should go or not go?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, Your Honours, and Mr. Prosecutor, it is the beginning of the Washington negotiations in which Croatia was directly involved at the behest of the international community. These talks started in Frankfurt, continued in Bonn, ended in Washington, concerning the so-called Washington negotiations. The international community asked for Croatia to be directly involved and Mr. Tudjman as well. You can see in the text that it is Mate Granic who is in charge of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to next go please to P 07516 in the second binder. P 07516. Sir, this is a record of a meeting at the presidential palace on the 7th of January, 1994, a few days later involving among others, perhaps, Mr. Tudjman, Granic, Akmadzic, Mr. Sancevic, and others. I'd like to direct your attention very quickly, please, to page 71. If you look at pages 71 and 72, sir, would you look at those please and would you agree with me that this illustrates you and others having a detailed conversation to actually agree on the language of certain draft documents? In English we might say you were wordsmithing the document, even choosing what particular words should be used; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, as I've already said, that Croatia was involved here and that the Washington Accords envisaged confederation between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and it is from that point of view that all aspects of these negotiations are being looked into.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in this particular occasion, you are talking about a scenario by which the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna would have the right to join the Republic of Croatia. At the end of that particular conversation, in fact at the end of that meeting -- no, I'm sorry, toward the end of the meeting on the bottom of page 72, for example, you even say, Mile Akmadzic: "I wouldn't use that 'whereas.'" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found that, regrettably. On what page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 72, on the bottom of page 72 of the transcript. Again, it should be the same in either the English or the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Mile Akmadzic here: "I wouldn't say, Mr. Matic, that, 'whereas.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in reference to the territorial claims that I asked you about a few moments ago, is it correct, sir, that you recall that at least in the earlier phases of your dealings in these matters, that the territory to be claimed by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the territory that should be -- that it should be encompass was something called the Hrvatska Banovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, sir. I can explain that if requested to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you testify in the Kordic case on page 20494 to 20495 on the 6th of June, 2000, the following: "In the beginning, before the Vance-Owen Plan was signed and before Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised, and before diplomatic relations were established, that all political solutions that were sought for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Tudjman mentioned that the Croat republic or rather the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna should in Bosnia and Herzegovina encompass those areas that belonged to" and it was transcribed "belonged to Srpska banovina in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For example," and I'm continuing the quote of your testimony, "For example, I was born in the Banovina Hrvatska. At the time that I was born, it was Banovina Hrvatska." That's the testimony that you gave under oath in the Kordic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "Serb" here is a mistake, that's a technical mistake. You've just read it out. There is another fact too. I was born on the 1st of October, 1939, when the banovina was in existence, Banovina Hrvatska, and that in contrast to that, I say and think, well, it is not a banovina now, it is not going to be a banovina just as it is not true that Mr. Prlic was born in the Socialist Republic of Croatia, rather, he was born in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall a man named Ivo Komsic and what position or functions did he hold in 1993 or if you can just briefly describe his involvement in events in Bosnia and Herzegovina during that time? Ivo Komsic.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina illegally replaced or dismissed Miro Lasic and Franjo Boras they chose Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Komsic instead of them. That is to say, irrespective of his resignation, Mr. Kljuic returned to the Presidency whereas Mr. Komsic who had not won the election joins the Presidency nevertheless. We have already discussed that during the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you attended a number of negotiation sessions in various locations including Geneva with Mr. Komsic during 1993 and 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Komsic often went to attend negotiations not within the delegation but as an accompanying group. He said that he was an expert by virtue of his profession for the political establishment of a state and from time to time, he made constructive suggestions for certain solutions especially for Central Bosnia that he hails from. In actual fact, I believe he was born in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in addition, then, to the other information you provided - thank you for that - but the answer then is yes, there were a number of occasions where you attended negotiation sessions where Mr. Komsic was also present?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few rounds of negotiations, not many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like you, please, to look at P 10508 in binder number 3. P 10508. 10508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Scott, we don't have such a number in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe its loose. Your Honour, I'm informed and I apologise, it's one of the loose documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. If the usher would ... To assist everyone it's on e-court now but to assist everyone still looking for it. It's 10508.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I think you have that now. Before I ask you a couple of questions about that document, let me just simply put it to you, sir, that isn't it true that throughout 1993 and into 1994, you continued to advocate a policy of ethnic cleansing, didn't you, of one form or another; that is, to either move Muslims out of so-called Croat areas or to sharply reduce their number?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit 10508, and this is an excerpt from Mr. Komsic's book in English translated as the title being "Survived Country, Who, When and Where, Divided BiH." And the Chamber has heard of this book and seen previous excerpts before. In the part that I've given to you, sir, and I think you should have it in both English and in Croatian, for the 27th of July, 1993, Mr. Komsic reports that, "We arrived in Geneva yesterday and stayed at the President Hotel. Boras and Akmadzic joined the Sarajevo delegation at the airport in Zagreb. Lasic invited me last night to his room for a discussion. Akmadzic and Boras were there." Skipping down because of time to -- toward the end of that first paragraph, "Akmadzic and Boras tried to convince me that it" I suggest to you that based on the context, the "it" consists of the interest of Croats and Croatia as a state which are referenced above, "Akmadzic and Boras tried to convince me that it was coming to be true on the grounds of the so-called Serb-Croat agreement which both Lasic and I challenged." Now, first of all, can you recall and describe to the Chamber what Serb-Croat agreement you were referring to around July 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to any agreement at all that involved the Serbs but not the Muslims. Not in that war, not then, not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put to you yesterday and I put to you again now: Do you recall that after the Vance-Owen Plan faded away, that by June of 1993, just a few weeks before this event on the 27th of July, that Tudjman and Izetbegovic had met again and had resurrected a plan to partition Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tudjman and Izetbegovic met --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... excuse me if I misspoke, Tudjman and Milosevic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting, therefore, I don't know. I do know that Tudjman and Izetbegovic met at least once a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then it goes on down -- further down the page and says, in the next paragraph, several sentences down, "Defending their respective positions, Boras and Akmadzic revealed that they still accepted the ethnic cleansing policy, but it had to be in the form of peaceful and 'voluntary moving.' They needed an agreement only for that purpose. They needed peace only to have the processes they had launched finalised in a different circumstances and without any force." Is that what you told Mr. Komsic on the 27th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. But I can explain. The policy that existed during the negotiations, and it wasn't just us, there was no ethnic cleansing, there would be no forcible movement and no one was to ban anyone else from moving and selecting their new place of residence. It shows that we weren't there to force anyone to go anywhere. It is obvious that Mr. Komsic misconstrued this meaning of this word here "voluntary." No one is to be banned from going wherever they like and choosing their own place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please go next to P 07260. P 07260 in the second binder. P 07260. I think most everyone has found that by now. Sir, if you can look at this record which is a transcript of a meeting again involving Mr. Tudjman and others at the presidential palace in Zagreb on the 19th of December, 1993. By way of just quick reference, let me ask you to go to page 16 of the document. Page 16, please. You are mentioned, I point you there because that among other places indicates your involvement in the meeting. Mile Akmadzic: "1.4 around Jajce and 0.5 beneath Stolac," which we'll come back to in a moment. But this was a meeting, sir, again with President Tudjman that you were involved in on the 19th of December, 1993. In the first part of the first several pages of the document 1 through 4, Mr. Tudjman, President Tudjman and Mr. Boban and others are talking about the release of Muslim prisoners from camps, HVO camps in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The middle of page 2, Boban reports among other things, "There isn't isn't a single camp left. It was finished at exactly on the evening of the 17th." President: "Issue a statement about it. Boban: "Reuters took all that news last night and it's been published." Going on over to page 3, bottom of page 3. Granic: "Mr. President, this is an excellent move, a very strong move which has had an impact and it should be exploited even further, therefore." Page 4, Boban: "CNN reported it last night." At the bottom of page 4, it appears that Mr. Tudjman again gives you an assignment. "Mile, write these things down so that you can use them." That was an instruction that President Tudjman gave to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was my question, sir. Was there anyone else named Mile in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was me. The Bosniaks and the Croats put me in charge of this when the negotiations began. The system of solving the Washington system but not that that I should draw up a paper based on which the Croat and the Muslim sides could reach an agreement. The Muslim delegation asked, while Mr. Redman was still the special envoy of the US President, that the Croats and Muslims were clashing, to a smaller extent, and that the Croats and Muslims would reach some common peace before a third party could be called in. It was to that effect that I was putting together a paper ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and to move on from that. In fact, in this same document if you go to page 15, please, page 15, President Tudjman turns to the topic of the ongoing meetings, negotiation meetings. President: "Let's move on to preparations for the meetings in Geneva and Brussels. We have to review two problem areas. One is the political agreement, so to speak, but we must review each formulation in detail. The second thing is our views about territorial demarcation. Akmadzic and Matic, have you studied each formulation?" Lower down on that page, "President: Let's agree on what we should first undertake. Perhaps it could be the territorial issue. The troops we need so that we don't all waste time. According to all these reports and what Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akmadzic heard during these negotiations, Owen and Stoltenberg are conducting negotiations in such a way that they are actually not fulfilling the task that the European Union gave them and that is that a further 3.3 per cent of territory should be given to the Muslims at the Serbs' expense. According to what Mr. Sarinic told me that they even wanted 1.9 or 2.3 per cent from Croatia." Then lower down the page it says, Sarinic looking at maps, and you can tell there everyone seems to be looking at maps, "Look these over, there were various maps." Then Akmadzic: "1.4 around Jajce and 0.5 beneath Stolac." What were though percentage numbers or referenced when you said "1.4 around Jajce and 0.5 beneath Stolac," what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about -- and Your Honours, of course, we were talking about how Croats and Muslims should reach 51 per cent of the territory that they are still holding. This was really about percentage where it would be more convenient for this to be part of the future of the federation, namely, Croats -- based on that international proposal that Croats, conditionally speaking, the territory 17.6 per cent; Muslims 33 per cent, and this is how one arrived in the various versions at the figure that was then agreed in Dayton, 49 versus 51, but that wasn't the agreement that we'd had in Washington. The agreement was for all those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina to belong to the federation where the predominantly Croat areas and the predominantly Muslim areas would be together which was about 58 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point I just wish to make one intervention. In the previous witness that we had, percentages were brought up and there was an objection by the Prosecution and I just wanted to draw this attention to the Court because when I tried to bring it up, the Prosecution claims there are no such discussions and here now he's using the very same piece of evidence that I was trying to do and I just want to show the supreme irony in all of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I don't know what event Mr. Karnavas is talking about. If we have time I'm sure that he and I can talk together and talk about which context he's talking about and I can see whether that's accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In any event, sir, later on page 16, Mr. Sarinic says, "There are three areas in which they, it's here, 1.4 per cent and 0.5 per cent here, that's the 1.9, or for all practical purposes, the 2 per cent where they're asking us to give up, and this is Caplina down here and here they wanted a corridor ..." And then if you continue over to page 18, top of page 18. President: "Yes, closer to Neum by the harbour by Celevo. The two of you have to have all this in order and present it in a well-argued manner so it is out of the question that Croatia could accept a territorial reduction." Now, do you recall what territorial reduction Mr. Tudjman was talking about in that instance?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what we're looking at here is the 17.6 per cent that had to be found for all the elements to be met that I've been telling you about, the ethnic criterion or the other criterion for determining those territories regardless of whether we're looking at the republic as it was at the time or the provinces later on or later on a joint Croat-Muslim agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look please next at page 20. At the top of that page, Mile Akmadzic: "Mr. President, the Muslims are not seeking these concessions. They are seeking concessions in western and eastern Bosnia. They are placing emphasis on the areas in which their people live. They are not interested in Kresevo ..." Then Sarinic makes a statement and then back to the president, "We are defending what's ours." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that with the Muslims what I stated and I see what the president said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where were you getting your information at that time in terms of what concessions the Muslims were or were not seeking?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the negotiations that were in progress everywhere. There is a reference here in Brussels, to Geneva, all sorts of negotiations and then we were reaching all the those conclusions, what and to whom, in one such I never used the word division of Bosnia. I was saying that Bosnia and Herzegovina had to comprise certain units and not be carved up into units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can next please turn to page 24. After the interventions of others, President Tudjman turns back to you, "President: Mile, what do you think?" Mile Akmadzic: "Mr. President, I think the same." This is after an intervention by Mr. Boban. My mistake, my apologies to the courtroom, if we can go back to page 23 so we can put this into context. Page 23, Boban says in the upper part of the page, "I'll tell you what I think and I'll back it up with arguments. This is the first time I'm saying this. There were 45.000 Muslims in Mostar before the war ..." and then he continues on with discussions about that. The next paragraph down he says, "I mean I would never accept that part of Mostar across the Neretva for 45.000 Muslims. Therefore, we can agree to the Neretva being a border." Now, in that context, if we go to page 24, "Mile, what do you think?" Akmadzic: "Mr. President, I think the same. But for proper consideration, we need two versions, one being the Neretva and Celevo and one is that solution down there. If we have the solution as the one down there, then it's acceptable too, provided that the border goes further along towards the Muslims and on towards Stolac from Buna and Blagaj up so we can eliminate them completely at least from Caplina." So what you were proposing in your discussions with President Tudjman is to at least "eliminate the Muslims from Caplina"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. That's not -- I'll let the witness answer because that's not exactly what I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you say -- is it reported here sir that "... from Buna and Blagaj up, so we can eliminate them completely at least from Caplina."

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't the way I put it. When we read this, it sounds ugly but I'm not that man and I think all the elements here show that I was moderate. Even elimination can have various meanings. However, I didn't use the word. And I return to you, Mr. Prosecutor, you, my testimony yesterday, when I was from Mr. Kordic, if you went through that you will realise that I made a whole lot of amendments. There could be errors that were made in situations such as these, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... top of page 25, Boban in response after you, the president was asking about the town of Mostar president: "Wait a minute. That's one question." So coming back to you. Mile Akmadzic: "It's better for us to partition the town than have 25 or 30.000 Muslims but we should seek compensation elsewhere." That's what you said, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. However, the division of Mostar was something that was envisaged in the Owen-Stoltenberg plan. It was always something that was on the agenda. This was something that was being arranged and then what happened happened under the terms of the Washington agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 25, Susak comes back in. "Mr. President, the problem is that they won't allow us when -- here you have Mostar and they take the airport. If they allow us a partition it will be along the Neretva; in other words, everything along the other side of the Neretva is in their hands." If you could then go on please to page 48, end of the meeting. President Tudjman gives you again another assignment, sir. Page 48 last entry. President: "All right. Find a formulation. Anything else? No. All right, gentlemen, I think those are the essential questions, but now the two of you, Matic and Akmadzic, each of you should review the formulations. Every comma needs to conform to this, while the rest of you should continue the meeting." Sir, did you then -- you and Mr. Matic after that continue to prepare the formulations giving attention, as President Tudjman told you to, to every comma?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. At this time I was writing up the papers for our final agreement with the Muslim side, the -- in our lingo we refer to this as the Croat-Muslim agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you next please go to P 07856 which will be in the second binder, binder number 2. P 07856. This is a meeting, sir, with President Tudjman again and others on the 13th of February, 1994. Just to set the scene, I will refer you to the first intervention or statement by the president on the first page. "Gentlemen, I told Minister Susak to invite Mate and the rest of you -- a summit of the leading people of Herceg-Bosna -- for us to come to an agreement as to how and what to take forward after all that has happened recently: Our general meeting in Livno, the Sarajevo meeting, the current talks in Geneva, but above all, regarding the new situation arising from the initiative taken by the United States with a group of European countries for an ongoing solution to the Bosnia-Herzegovinian crisis." The reference to a new situation, that was a reference to the Washington agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as I said, let's take it step-by-step. Even in the earlier minutes and then onwards from there and now we're going towards the Washington agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What had happened, sir, is it correct that by the end of 1993, by early 1994, Owen-Stoltenberg was displaced, if you will, or knocked off the table by a new proposal being advocated as stated here by the United States and certain European countries which became known as "Washington"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but there was no clear division between the plans. As soon as we realised that one plan was failing then we would take it from there step-by-step and here we're dealing with the Washington agreement to -- in proper, the future Washington agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you please to go to page 42. The middle of that page President Tudjman says, "If we do not have them all, for five, then we can say 5.500 and we can go with that." I will pause here and say that in the context of the top part of the page and back to page 41, the topic is the number of Croatians killed as a result of the conflicts with the Muslims and Serbs. The number suggested that in the conflict with the Serbs, approximately 2500 and in the conflicts with the Muslims, approximately 5.500. Tudjman goes on to say, "So more than two times the number with the Serbs and it is likely that these Croatian people of ours would not consent to simply remain in a union with the Muslims, or please, what do you think, would you consent and the people in Herceg-Bosna?" Akmadzic: "I will give my opinion first and then, however, it seems that the direction of world events is such that ..." Tudjman: "Forget about the direction of world events for starters ..." And then you go on to say at the top of page 43, "Our basic goal is Herceg-Bosna with borders, with the war behind us, however we put it but I think there should not be particular problems with not living in the union and here we would back out from this union of three -- so that we can live together with the Muslims, together in the way that I mean -- in our own republic, our interests protected, protected from their people, independent but in some relationship, but we cannot be in a relationship like the union. They have a larger population. We thought about that now in Geneva, we have Croatia behind us, they have the mass behind them. But our tight connection with Croatia must be present in all variations and our separation from the Muslims in all variations." That was what you stated as your basic goal; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite, but the goal was achieved. For one to keep both one's national rights and not to go into a unitary state but a decentralised Bosnia and Herzegovina together with the Muslims and together with the Serbs, if possible, it is my position, this is our position and it remained unchanged throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Then if you will go on, please, to page 46. Page 46 and 47 there is an intervention by Jadranko Prlic. "Mr. President, the information which was presented today is exceptionally important, and of strategic importance,." And jumping to the end of that paragraph and touching on something that we have discussed in your testimony, Mr. Prlic says, "I mean, it is a fact that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina have different policies, different interests, in fact, depending on where they live." Going over to page 47, "Despite all the information, we have created a state in Herceg-Bosna with all systems including customs and finance. People are born and die with Herceg-Bosnian documents. I think we should weigh all the elements carefully. Absolutely no solution is acceptable without a Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna, i.e., a Croatian republic, and the borders should encompass as many areas as possible in the whole of Central Bosnia. I believe we can achieve this by military means, if necessary, in order to make sure that these things are developing the way they are developing, but they are developing favorably nonetheless. They have been crushed militarily after all." Now, when Mr. Prlic makes reference to "they have been crushed militarily after all," who was he referring to, if you remember or can assist us with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Prlic means the Muslims, then he probably means the Muslims, but I do not realise that they were crushed militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, Mr. Prlic goes on to say that in reference to around this time, Mr. Boban being removed which we haven't touched on yet in these documents although they are part of these transcripts but we don't have time to cover all of the topics. In the reference to that, Mr. Prlic goes on to say, "We are demanding that their symbols, Alija," which I take it to be a reference to Mr. Izetbegovic "and Silajdzic step down. Only then might different trends emerge among them too. I have prepared some other proposals. The moment is extremely critical. That's my estimate of the situation down there. Let this international thing blow over. I believe we will have -- there won't be an authority that will be able to keep the situation under control. That's my estimate." Do you recall any discussions around this time of again demanding that Izetbegovic and Silajdzic be removed from their positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that, but Izetbegovic and Silajdzic were very hardline as far as the Muslim people were concerned. It was very difficult to negotiate with them so I assume that this is what this is all about. I did not attend this meeting. I went to catch a plane in order to get to the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go please, next to page 68. And this is continuing with Tudjman talking which I think the record will show he began talking on page 66. We're now at page 68. In that first part of the page he says, "... and you, too, and Herceg-Bosna have to be aware of this but this also means that we must not abandon our most essential goals. It means that we cannot abandon the goal of establishing the republic of Herceg-Bosna and we will see how it will be established. In a military sense, it is clear to us that it is in our interest to maintain control over the territory we have at present ..." He goes on to say that this is a matter for further discussion. Now, the meeting then turns to the topic of selecting the new leadership of Herceg-Bosna. On page 69, Boban says, "We're talking about a president and two vice-presidents." Then if you would jump, please, to page 86. There is a continuing discussion of this same topic and Mr. Sancevic intervenes and says, Well, we should have a few Muslims as well. At the end of that intervention by Mr. Sancevic says "We need a few Muslims to show that it's a democratic thing." Then continuing over to page 87, Mr. Pasalic raises what he perceives as a problem because he says, "Well, actually, Mr. Tudjman, President Tudjman, the constitution or fundamental decision of Herceg-Bosna does not allow for this thing called a presidential council." Do you recall these discussions at which Tudjman and the other representatives from Croatia, Mr. Pasalic and others were involved in selecting both the structure and the members of the new government for Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that and as I've already said, I don't think I attended this part of the meeting; however, I do know these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention very quickly, because I want to finish up here in the next few minutes, to page 90. Tudjman concludes this part of the discussion. On page 90, Tudjman says, "Don't try to pull legal tricks. We are at war and just say that the function of the president will be carried out by the presidential council." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already explained that, that at that time, the presidential council had taken over the function that Mr. Boban had had previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. That was my question to you. So in fact, following this meeting, the presidential council was put in place at which a number of people were placed to form the new presidential body, if you will, in place of Mr. Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next ask you to turn to Exhibit P 08012. It should be in the second binder again, P 08012. Sir, this is another meeting at the presidential palace on the 4th of March, 1994. We see a list of at least some of the people present at the meeting, apparently including yourself. Actually, I should indicate at the top of this page it says it's the 37th session or meeting of the VONS. You said a few minutes ago that the VONS was the security body and that you recalled attending it at least on one occasion. So perhaps you recall this being the one occasion, on the 4th of March, 1994, that you attended.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I attended two meetings. I couldn't remember but now that I see this, I think I attended two. This one plus another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on the bottom of the first -- excuse me, the bottom of the second page, again there is a reference to you and Mr. Zubak coming from the Washington talks. And on the top of page 3, just so we can know that -- who else was involved, Tudjman says, "I mentioned these two, and Mr. Prlic is also here." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 4, Tudjman goes on talking and about the middle of that page, he says, "That's what I've been talking about in a message yesterday, and if somebody doesn't understand, I say why did we create the Croat republic of Herceg-Bosnia, then I'll say it again, so we could achieve the results of this politics. If we didn't have and don't have now the Croat republic of Herceg-Bosna, we wouldn't have Croat-Muslim federation in Bosnia. That is, we wouldn't have the confederation of that Croat-Muslim Bosnia with Croatia." "In other words, we'll have in the sphere of Croatia, I will not say two Croatias, we'll have at least half of Bosnia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that what's happening in this meeting and other meetings around this time is that Tudjman is trying to sell -- he is trying to sell what has been a fairly substantial shift that's no longer Owen-Stoltenberg and it's no longer a separate Croat republic but now it's Washington agreement and Tudjman is trying to convince those around him that, well, in fact, this is a good deal. Isn't that what's happening here?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a free interpretation. It can be understood that way too. However, the confederation between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina was proposed by the international community and the Washington Accords and in the Dayton Accords. Dayton involves special relations as well. Now, there are no special relations or confederation that are functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my time has almost expired. Let me ask you, please, to look at page 23. At the middle of that page, the president intervenes, thanks the previous speaker, "Thank you." Then he turns apparently to you, Akmadzic. Mile Akmadzic: "I think we can be happy and satisfied how president of Republic of Croatia and president of Croats, Mr. Doctor Franjo Tudjman had access to the whole depth and essence of this problem with which we are now dealing and about which we are talking. I would also like to say that he was excellent last night -- president's addressing nation was accepted among people with complete trust and understanding." Going over to page 24, middle of the page, you continue, "I believe that the most important thing now is that all of us who are directly involved in talks understood and led by President Tudjman, we understand what the world is asking from us." If you go to page 29. This is you talking, sir, you began talking previously on page 23 and continued at the middle of the page, "However, we must know at this moment this is the only solution; in my opinion, the best one so far. I would say here, that I met with some, Mr. Zubak and I, met with some of our Americans in Frankfurt," et cetera. Then jumping a couple of sentences, you say, "We Croats in BH wished and are still wishing to be completely behind Croatia, with Croatia, to be in the same state. However, I believe that the other part of the solution offering confederation, solves that issue at this moment in a best possible way, and there will be Croats both in BH and Croatia, and that that's for the well-being of all Croats. Thank you." Sir, when you said this is the best solution solving that issue at this moment, what did you mean by saying "at this moment"? What did you see beyond that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the agreement between the Croats and the Muslims, that they should be together in one state and that they should have very close relations with Croatia, roughly the way things are today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you will turn to page 49, please. Mr. Prlic intervenes and says, "First, I think that the agreement is a reasonable solution but, of course, not a final solution." It goes on from there. Can we take it again, sir, that those of you from Herceg-Bosna, you, Mr. Prlic and others, saw this as a stepping stone to something else but not -- did not represent the desired final solution; isn't that correct? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] I think that it is impermissible to interpret words in this way. First of all, the Prosecutor is not reading the second sentence out and that sentence clearly states what I meant in the first sentence. He is manipulating something that is very clear. Let me use English or our own language. "First of all, I think that the agreement is a reasonable solution but it's not a final solution." Then the second question. "It is only a basis for an overall solution because at this point in time, we practically have under control almost the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is occupied. If we take the Serb part," and so on and so forth. So a year and a half after that, the Dayton agreement took place and things are quite clear. It is the tenth time today or so that the Prosecutor is distorting the very clear words that I uttered and that are part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... transcript, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As Mr. Prlic indicated second sentence of that particular paragraph goes on too say, "It's only a base for complete solution because we now control almost the whole territory of BH which is occupied." Now, if you could go on to page 55, please, and just concluding, Your Honours, in the next one or two minutes. On page 55, Tudjman then goes on and talks about -- perhaps you can confirm to us that it was known, was it not, that Mr. Mesic and Manolic had had great differences of opinion with President Tudjman about his policy towards Bosnia. You will see here that Mr. Tudjman turns his attention to them. Before we get to that specific part, though, if you will please look at the bottom of page 55 where Tudjman says, "I was the one who mainly initiated suggestion of Cutileiro's canton solution and took Vance and Owen to the isles of Brijuni in order to obtain such a suggestion for a solution of provinces which would be in this sense and this as well, et cetera and this -- for confederate solution with union, et cetera." Did you understand that to be, based on all your knowledge, sir, and your involvement, your close involvement in these events, that it was Mr. Tudjman who had played this role in Cutileiro as he describes and concerning Vance-Owen?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in the Cutileiro plan, I've already explained that over here. As for the Vance-Owen Plan, it was a plan that first of all involved peace talks in the territory of all of the former Yugoslavia. The most important plenary sessions were attended by Tudjman, Milosevic, Cosic, no, not Cosic but these were peace talks that had to do with the territory of all of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Last page I will refer you to, sir, page 57, please. President Tudjman continues talking and about the middle of that page says, "Therefore, this is the difference and, please, Susak is right. We cannot face our public now due to political reasons, in order to prevent demoralisation among people who sacrificed themselves," et cetera. Sir, I put to you a few moments ago and is it not correct that this is again -- the problem that's being identified here by Tudjman and Susak is, look, this represents a substantial shift from the policy and goals that we've been pursuing and it's going to be -- it's going to cause some difficulty and we're going to have to sell this; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your comment and I am not in a position to comment on that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, do you recall when he said this, "We cannot face our public now due to political reasons ..." What did you understand Mr. Tudjman to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this here, I could give an interpretation to the effect that the public perhaps believed that they would get a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna that was being extinguished by way of this agreement and a joint Muslim-Croat federation was being established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to thank you for your testimony, for coming to The Hague and staying as long as you have. And I'd also like to thank the Chamber for giving me the additional time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quarter past 12.00. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the Trial Chamber would like to deliver an oral decision on the motion made by Ms. Alaburic. Having considered the witness's responses or answers to the questions put by the Prosecutor, the Chamber believes that circumstances are such that there could be -- that there will not be additional questions put by the Petkovic Defence. With respect to additional questions put by the Prlic Defence, of course the Prlic Defence is entitled to put any questions that it wishes to do but that will be taken into account as far as the global time is concerned. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I should say, Mr. Akmadzic.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were the prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I want to ask you: Were you ever questioned by the Office of the Prosecution as a suspect for ethnic cleansing or being engaged in a joint criminal enterprise? I put this question to you because today you have been accused of being a war criminal in the sense of ethnically cleansing. So have they ever come and questioned you as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in any way. Not outside the court, not inside this courtroom and not during my evidence in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, I would ask that the record, to use the Prosecution's phrase, be cleansed or stricken of any insinuation that this man was involved in ethnic cleansing because it was put to him, he was accused, they have a responsibility given his position as prime minister, he would actually hold a high position and if this Tribunal is here to prosecute the most serious and we're talking about ethnic cleansing, then they either had a responsibility to investigate, indict and prosecute or not make such serious allegations before this Tribunal and before Your Honours. So at this point, I put this and you can deliberate at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Akmadzic, concerning Sarajevo, you were asked when you left. Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber so they can understand what it was like to be in Sarajevo in December or November of 1992, and how it was to try to run government sessions, Presidency sessions, how to run a country in that city at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, speaking in your own words, the question is put and answered. It was answered in a very emotional and very impressive way on direct. Really, I remember the witness even taking a cloth to his eyes and I was moved by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- precisely and I was wondering why the Bench didn't react and say that's been asked and answered, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe they are less emotional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well, if the Trial Chamber is satisfied, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were asked specifically or the insinuation was that you abandoned Sarajevo. And then you were shown a document and I believe it was P 10473, where it was a newspaper article where Haris Silajdzic took over your position, the absentee Croat predecessor as the document said. We don't need to look at the document, Mr. Usher, but I want to ask you this question concretely: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber where was Silajdzic in 1992? How often was he in Sarajevo? What he was doing and how often did he report to you or to his -- to your predecessor when he was Minister of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Silajdzic was spending practically all his time abroad. He never came to any government meetings. He never submitted any reports. He once spoke to me but not more than once. I told him he could not not travel abroad without the government's authorisation and without previously conferring with me. He accepted that but the very next day he went to the conference of Islamic countries in Jed [phoen]. So throughout all of 1992 and most of 1993, he was abroad. But he was a party to the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked some questions and you were shown some documents concerning some discussions about certain percentages, how to reach 33 per cent and so on; do you recall that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you alluded to it but I want to make sure that we know concretely the facts. Was this discussion also not taking place at Dayton?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- I wasn't there but that's where the present percentage was agreed, 49 versus 51. Many of the talks involved figures but the situation on the ground would often change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was not in trying to reach these magical percentages, wasn't -- it wasn't based on population but it was based on where to draw the lines within Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, but the population in Bosnia and Herzegovina was also taken into account, the respective percentages, what the Croats had, what the others had, and that was one of the criteria, the Croats had 17.6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were the internationals aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the ones positing this. It came from them. They led the negotiations in a way and we were all involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did the Muslims, did they, too, look at maps and try to decide what part of the 33 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina they wanted for their peoples?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were involved as well, but there is another thing that I wish to say here that I have not said so far. Mr. Izetbegovic at one point said that he would agree to a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina falling to Croatia. The question was how big. But we never asked for that and we never accepted that. But he was the one actually pondering the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at what Izetbegovic said at one of these meetings. This is a tape recording of a Presidency meeting held on January 14, 1994, if may have the usher's assistance, we saw this document on 15 January 2007. My God, we've been in this trial for that long -- actualy, it's 2008 is when we saw this. In fact, if we go back to the transcript, it would be on page 26.294 but I have the actual document here and I'm going to read a portion to you and ask you to comment on it because it deals with this issue of percentages. The page is marked for you, it's page 19 of the document, Your Honours. Let's see what Izetbegovic said. Page 19. You will see that there is a red sticker, sir, that's the page. We marked it for you so you can find it easily. Here what Izetbegovic said: "Let us all understand, all these talks we had including republics and 33 per cent, et cetera, nothing of it has been determined because Klaus warned me when I talked about some things he said, 'You know, Mr. Izetbegovic, the rule about politics: Until we agree on everything, we agree on nothing.' So, so far we have not agreed on anything. These are all just preconditions for some agreement. Of course, if it suits us, we can go back to the beginning. We only have to ask ourselves if we have better solution. But as soon as we see that we are better off, turn everything back to the beginning." Now, I ask you, Mr. Akmadzic, does this not sound like the negotiating tactics of Izetbegovic that you experienced throughout that period? And I put this question specifically because of the questions put to you yesterday about some opera singing ending the show, and I'm referring to that rather coarse approach of suggesting someone of a healthy weight size not having sung.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're putting to me is correct, I think it is correct. That's precisely how Mr. Izetbegovic was behaving during the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further redirect. Sir, I want to thank you and I want to apologise for keeping you longer than I had predicted, especially during the European cup season which I know that you are a very big fan of football. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to be given an opportunity to address the Chamber just very briefly with no questions asked. It is my deepest conviction, Your Honours, as a state official of Bosnia and Herzegovina who held a number of different posts that Croats and Muslims fought each other in Bosnia and Herzegovina but it was never termed a war, it was always termed a conflict. The Croats and Muslims in Bosnia are -- have very close links to one another. They established the fact that there was a war there and they provided a joint definition of this war. The Croatian democratic community is not, as is sometimes believed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a branch of Croatia's HDZ. Quite the contrary, it's an independent party. And this is often the case with other political parties across Europe. They entertain very close links to Croatia's HDZ. The Party for Democratic Action have its origin in Bosnia and Herzegovina but there have a -- there is a party called that in Croatia and it's represented in Croatia's parliament. Throughout this war as a whole and throughout the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims there was the Croatian embassy in Bosnia and Herzegovina that kept on operating throughout as did the BH embassy in Croatia. Throughout this war the mosque in Croatia had an Islamic centre that was considered to be the largest of its kind in Europe, the largest of its kind in Europe. And it went on operating smoothly. A year ago, I believe, it was at that Islamic centre that a large conference was held at which the BH raise their -- the highest ranking religious official, Ceric, praised the relations between the Croats and the Muslims in the most complimentary terms. I think Croatia was the first country in Europe that recognised Islam as an official religion enjoying equal rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we gave you an opportunity to speak but just a few words but now you are starting pleadings and I must interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Your Honours all the same. This is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of my colleagues and myself, I thank you. I join Mr. Karnavas in his thanks. Thank you for coming to testify in The Hague. My very best wishes for your return to your country and I shall ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, can we start the next witness in order to not waste time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we don't have more than one binder? I'm disappointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wait until the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Could you state your first name, surname and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Zarko Primorac, the 15th of September, 1937.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not entirely sure we got the date correct because the witness is standing too far from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation or don't you have any.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an economist, I have a BA in economy. I now work with a company in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your date of birth, is it the 15th of September, 1937?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had an opportunity to testify before a court of law as to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this going to be the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated. Some brief explanation from me. You're about to answer questions first by Mr. Karnavas, then you will answer questions possibly by other Defence counsel as part of their cross-examination. Thereafter, the Prosecutor, who is seated to your right-hand side will also ask questions of you as part of the cross-examination. The Judges seated in front of you may also have questions for you but we do it when there is a document that really calls for follow-up questions, mainly. Do endeavour to be concise and brief in your answers. We have breaks every hour and a half. We break for 20 minutes. We only have three-quarters of an hour left because we're going to break at quarter to 2.00. You've just made an oath to testify. You are now a witness of the Court. In other words, you may not contact the Prlic Defence any longer. This being said, you have the floor, Mr. Karnavas, for 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, and my apologies for keeping you waiting. I will first begin by asking you some questions about your background and with the Court's permission, I will just lead you through your background and if you could just validate whether what I'm saying is correct and then we will get into the documents. You told us that you were born in 15 September 1937, and as I understand it, you were received a Ph.D in economics in 1976 in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Since then, you've attended other international seminars as well as in 1995, you passed the exam to become an authorised auditor as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during your 35 years of experience in working as an economist you have also been the president of the municipality of assembly in Citluk and that would have been in 1965 to 1969?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll skip through some of your other accomplishments and go into -- from 1969 to '72 you were a senior advisor of the general director of Energoinvest in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You then went on to become the general director for finance in the same company from 1972 to 1974 and then you were also the general director, and this would have been for non-ferrous metals, again for the same company from 1975 to 1981?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: All correct. But it wasn't called the general director, it was called the main director, the position. And the one between 1974 and 1981 was about non-ferrous metals, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at one point, you were also involved in the chamber of commerce of -- this would have been the chamber of commerce of what, Yugoslavia, or Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: I was a professional head of Sarajevo's chamber of commerce, that was 1981 to 1984 but at the same time, I was a member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia's chamber of commerce. Later, I was a member of the chamber of commerce of Bosnia and Herzegovina but not on a professional basis. On a professional basis, I was working only for the Sarajevo chamber of commerce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then from 1984 to 1998 you were the vice-president of the steering board of Energoinvest and then later on, you became the vice-president of the steering board from 1989 to 1992 prior to taking up your post as minister of finance for the Republic of BiH which you held from June to December 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some dates to correct. Between 1984 and 1989, not 1988. Vice-chairman of steering board, although it was called the business board of the Energoinvest under the rules. And then between 1991 and 1992, I was the deputy president. So it's just the dates about the first job. It wasn't 1988, it was 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, on page 83, lines 2 and the following, you are reported as asking and I heard it like that, "From 1984 to 1998 you were the vice-president of the steering board of Energoinvest and then later on, you became the vice-president of the steering board."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should have been 1984 to 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, but twice vice-chairman of the steering board?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There were two and we can -- I can ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're clarifying, at page 81, line 21, the witness states he was born in 1937. I wonder, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he has more hair than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Don't bring hair into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could clarify for us the positions that you held with Energoinvest from 1984 to, say, 1992, if you could just tell us that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: I -- in large companies of Yugoslavia there, the managing body was normally called board. I was the vice chairman between 1984 and 1989 and then I was the deputy chairman of the business board or the board between 1989 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And then after you became -- after you left the Ministry of Finance in BiH which would have been in December of 1992, as I understand it, you began working for yourself starting an auditing company, auditing consulting company in Zagreb which you later -- which was later bought up by Price Waterhouse. And it was after that period that you became a special advisor and eventually a member of the board of directors of Price Waterhouse Coopers in Zagreb and that would have been in 1998 to 2001 when you became the board member -- member of the board and director in Price Waterhouse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Too many questions all at once. I'll try to clarify it for you in the following way. I, along with a couple of my fellow colleagues, established a company that did auditing and consulting. The company was then bought up by Price Waterhouse in 1997. I became a special consultant for them. They then merged with Coopers in 1998. And they became Price Waterhouse Coopers. I was a manager in that company up until 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you continued working after that period, and today, in your field that is, and today as I understand it you are the regional chairman in Deloitte, is that correct, in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: That's correct, it's a non-executive position. It's called chairman but it's not an executive position. What I do is market communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And aside from all of this in the meantime, you've also been a professor of economics, you taught approximately 15 years, as I understand it, in Sarajevo. The subjects would have been finance, economics systems and policy in Yugoslavia, financial management; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm not going to list all your accomplishments because they're quite many but in addition to some of the professional activities that you've been involved with, you've been a member of the organising committee of the world banking congress in Dubrovnik in 1989?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it at some point you might have even been involved in the Winter Olympics that were held in Sarajevo in 1984 in some capacity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the chairman of the Sarajevo chamber of commerce and I was a member of the Organising Committee of the 14th Winter Olympic Games.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And in addition to this you've published approximately 100 articles in your field and, as I understand it, you are an author of a couple of books and have edited the Croatian Financial Guide 1995, 1998, 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. A small correction of the interpretation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the nature of the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the correction, sir, so we have it on the record?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: The interpreter said members instead of articles, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, and just a couple more questions about your background. As I understand it, you've never been a member of HDZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But prior to the break-up of Yugoslavia, if we can put it at that, you were a member of the Communist League, is that what it was called?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it was called and yes, I was a member of the Communist League of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that based on your experience both as an economist, as a professor and being involved in the various organisations, that you have a pretty good understanding of how a country's economy functions and how the financial institutions work?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: I think I have a pretty good understanding of how Yugoslavia's economy functioned before the war. And I think I have a good understanding of how the economy works today especially in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally, if you could just tell us -- because -- from our conversation you had indicated that on several occasions, various offers had been -- had come your way concerning positions either at the state level, at the Yugoslav level or at the republic level. Could you just list some of those positions that you were offered and you rejected in order to stay into the private sector?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Between 1989 and 1990 and 1991, I had several offers to join the work of political organisations, among others, Ante Markovic invited me to nominate me as a member of the federal executive council. I had been nominated officially by Bosnia and Herzegovina for that position. It was for personal reasons that I had to turn this down. At the same time, I received several nominations in Bosnia and Herzegovina to various positions, I received an invitation to become the member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I refused that too because I wanted to continue to work in my field and in the economy because that had held a far greater interest for me than to go into politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, with that, the first two documents -- and Your Honours, I must apologise they are not in order but just one binder so I think we'll manage. The first two documents, just very quickly, these are housekeeping matters and I will be referring to 1D 02645 if you have it, it's dated 15 June 1992. 1D 02645. I just wanted to bring it to everyone's attention that if we go to page 4, for instance, in English, it says, "Members and ministers of the government of RBH were appointed as follows ..." and we see your name under number 5. So this would have been page 4 in the English section and page 4 in the B/C/S. That's what we call all three languages for convenience sake. So it was on or about 15 June 1992 when you took up your position as -- in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct? Or finance, I'm sorry, Minister of Finance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Correct. But I have another small correction to make about the date. The date here on these minutes says the 15th of June, 1992. The minutes from a meeting of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I remember, we were nominated and we took our solemn vows on the 18th of June, 1992. It was three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Following our nominations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the next document is 1D 01632. Again just for housekeeping purposes, 1632. And that may be towards the end of your binder, Your Honours, because this is dated -- 1D 01632, this is dated 23 December 1992. It's a decision and this is when you were relieved of your post as a member of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Correct. That is the decision. I would prefer to opt for the determine "dismissed" rather than relieved because that is what the document suggests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So are you suggesting that you were dismissed as opposed to being relieved?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: No, it's the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we talk about your tenure as the Minister of Finance, I want to deal with three particular documents that were authored by my client and this would have been prior to the break-up or prior to the conflict, I should say. The first document is 1D 02356, I will just sort of read a section or a couple of sentences and ask you to comment in general about the situation to see whether Mr. Prlic's take on the events as he was publicising it to the folks back then were more or less reflective of the time. 1D 02356. Okay. We can see at the top he is a member of the -- he is the vice-president of the republican executive council of Bosnia and Herzegovina on economic reforms. Did you know what this republican executive council was?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Speaking in present-day terms, it was the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the second paragraph, he's talking about that there is a problem with liquidity and then he goes on to say, "In this year, 1500 legal entities with about 37.000 employed were unable to meet their obligations." Further down, basically he's talking about the economy as it was back then. Can you tell us whether that more or less reflected the situation as it existed back then? Can you tell us a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was rather difficult. After Markovic was elected federal prime minister, the prime minister of Yugoslavia, he initiated a reform that was supposed to resolve many problems that had existed in the Yugoslav economy until then. However, as a matter of fact during the first few months, it yielded some good results especially in terms of slowing down or doing away with inflation altogether, if I can put it that way, but after a few months, I can't tell he exactly how many months, at least after six or nine months after he became prime minister, things started getting increasingly complicated. The old problems of the Yugoslav economy returned. The inability of Yugoslav companies to pay their bills was at a very high level so in general terms, that is correct looking at this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And -- staying with the same document, if we look at the very last page, he says that, "It would be necessary to strengthen state authorities by radical measures. We have taken over the financing of the judiciary so that the secretary of interior will soon be receiving funds from the budget." Then he goes on to say that the municipalities need to be -- shall be divested of certain functions. And then the last paragraph he recommends the establishment of a fund for development. Given the circumstances at the time, were these more or less the sorts of measures that an economist, a progressive economist would be thinking of in trying to deal with the situation as it existed back then, and we're talking prior to the break-up or prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: Please allow me to read this. Yes, the Bosnian economy, the economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina had greater problems than the economy, say, of Slovenia and Croatia had although they were part of the overall Yugoslav economy because the Bosnian economy primarily relied on the production of energy resources, timber processing, the so-called primary sector, as it were. According to the rules of the game that were in force in that system, these energy resources were delivered to the more developed republics and the prices of these energy resources were fixed for the most part and that is why the economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina had even greater difficulties. Mr. Prlic tried to get things moving. The fund for development was a good idea at the time. I don't know but I assume that this idea on the establishment of public companies is motivated by the thesis implying the resolution of the problem of fixed prices of energy and raw materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And very quickly with the next document, the next two documents again dealing with more or less the same period. This one is dated 11 January 1991. The previous one wasn't and that's why I made reference to his position. Here, Dr. Prlic is asked about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you would facilitate us the task of following if you gave the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. You're absolutely right. 1D 02232. 2232. If you look at this document, it says that it's the -- the journalist is asking Dr. Prlic about the Republic of Serbia's rating of the Yugoslav payment system and Dr. Prlic says, "I think we can conclude that this is a decision that has been taken, a move that has been made which is unprecedented in monetary history, an act of state crime that is directed at other parts of Yugoslavia." It says, "In this regard, I'm recommending that we should send a telex to the federal executive council seeking vigorous measures, i.e., demanding that the monetary effects on other areas of Yugoslavia be neutralised."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down? Thank you. And one mike is open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know what Dr. Prlic is talking about in this occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC
utterances.text: I think I do know. This had to do with what we called an incursion into the monetary [Realtime transcript read in error "monastery"] system of Yugoslavia. Now what was this all about? At one point in time, Serbia, Milosevic headed the state at the time, at one point in time, could -- Serbia could not afford to pay retirement pensions to its pensioners. They simply didn't have the money to do that. Then through the public accounting service, there was a state institution for monetary transactions, Serbia actually made an incursion. I cannot give you the exact figure but I remember that the figure the people talked about was 1.400.000.000. I cannot be sure but it probably had to do with several hundred million dollars. And in this way, the Republic of Serbia broke into the monetary system and paid these pensions at the expense of everybody else in Yugoslavia. Now I as an economist could say that as a fact this incursion, as it were, into the monetary system was the beginning of the disintegration of the monetary system of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
